scenes.narration: Six point nine billion dollars. That is how much America's airports earned in a single year from parking and ground transportation. More than passenger airlines paid them to land their planes.

Think about what that means. Before your plane even leaves the ground, the airport has already been paid. For your parking spot. Through a charge hidden in your ticket. In rent from the airline. And for the coffee you bought at the gate.
So who actually owns these giant machines, and how do they make their money?
By the end of this video, you will know the four ways an airport gets paid. Your ticket, the airlines, your car, and the terminal itself.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with a surprise. Most big American airports are not companies. According to the Government Accountability Office, many are owned by states, counties, cities or public authorities. And when they take federal grants, they promise to run the airport to be as self-sustaining as possible, and to spend the airport's money on the airport.

scenes.narration: That is a big business. According to the Federal Aviation Administration's financial reports, the airports that have reported so far earned at least thirty-four point five billion dollars in operating revenue in twenty twenty-five. They also carried about one hundred and forty-one billion dollars of debt, money borrowed to build terminals, runways and garages. And they counted almost a billion passenger boardings, nine hundred and ninety-six million, in a single year.

And the customers keep coming. Airlines carried about one point one billion passengers to, from and within the United States in twenty twenty-five. On November thirtieth, twenty twenty-five, the TSA screened more than three point one million people in a single day, the highest number in its records.

Let me draw how an airport is built. Here is the city or authority that owns it. It borrows money with bonds. It builds a terminal and runways. Then it collects money from everyone who uses them, and uses that money to pay back the debt. A public owner, run like a business.

scenes.narration: The first payment starts before you even arrive. It is hidden in the price of your ticket.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: It is called the passenger facility charge. Airports can add up to four dollars and fifty cents for each flight segment you take from them, up to eighteen dollars on a round trip. The airport keeps it, to pay for projects like new gates and runways. The cap was last raised in two thousand, from three dollars.

Small amounts, multiplied by hundreds of millions of passengers. In twenty twenty-five, these charges raised about three point eight five billion dollars. Since the program began in the nineteen nineties, they have raised seventy-nine point four billion dollars. Every large airport now charges the maximum.

And that is only one of the extras. There is a federal ticket tax of seven point five percent, a segment fee of five dollars and thirty cents per flight, and a security fee of five dollars and sixty cents per one-way trip. By our calculation, on a three hundred dollar round trip with a connection each way, all of these add up to about seventy-two dollars and ninety cents. Even on a nonstop round trip, it is about fifty-three dollars. Only the facility charge goes to the airport.

Airports want more. Their industry group argues that inflation has eaten away at the four fifty charge, and that it should rise to twelve dollars per passenger. The same group estimates that America's airports need about one hundred and seventy-four billion dollars of new investment over the next five years. That is the airports' own estimate. For now, the cap set in two thousand still stands.

Let me draw your ticket. Here is the fare the airline sets. On top, the ticket tax. Then the segment fees. Then the security fee. And here, a thin slice, the facility charge that goes straight to the airport. The price you see on the screen is many prices stacked together.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: The second payment comes from the airlines themselves. And it is the biggest of all.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: An airport is a landlord. Airlines rent gates, counters and offices, and pay a fee every time a plane lands. In twenty twenty-five, landing fees from passenger airlines brought in about five point five billion dollars. Terminal rents and fees brought in almost nine billion more. All the aviation charges together came to about nineteen point three billion dollars, more than half of operating revenue, by our calculation.

Airports measure this as the cost per enplaned passenger, what airlines pay the airport for every passenger who boards. In twenty twenty-five, across the airports that reported, it averaged about fifteen dollars and seventy-six cents. A cost that, one way or another, ends up in the price of your ticket.

Look at Los Angeles International. Its biggest source of revenue in its last financial year was terminal rent, about nine hundred and thirty-five million dollars. Second came landing fees, about three hundred and sixty-nine million. By our calculation, aviation charges made up about three quarters of the airport's operating revenue. The airlines are the anchor tenants of the whole operation.

Let me draw the lease. The airport builds the terminal. The airline rents the gate. Every landing pays a fee. And in many airports, the airlines sign long agreements that help the airport borrow money for new projects, because lenders know the rent will keep coming.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: But some of the most reliable money has nothing to do with planes. It comes from your car.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Parking and ground transportation brought America's airports six point nine billion dollars in twenty twenty-five. By our calculation, that is about one in every five dollars of operating revenue, and more than airlines paid in landing fees. It is the single biggest source of money that has nothing to do with flying. And it is growing. A year earlier, the same line was about six point five five billion dollars.

Then come the rental cars. Rental companies paid airports about two and a half billion dollars, not counting the extra facility charges added to rental contracts. At Los Angeles, parking was the third biggest revenue source of all, about one hundred and sixty-one million dollars, ahead of rental cars, restaurants and duty free.

Even ride-hailing pays. Los Angeles lists transportation network companies, the ride apps, among its top ten revenue sources, at about thirty-six million dollars a year. Whether you drive, rent or get dropped off, the airport collects.

Let me draw the curb. Here is the garage, charging by the hour. Here is the rental car center, paying a share of every contract. Here is the pickup lane, where every ride app pays a fee. Three ways to arrive, three ways to pay the airport.

scenes.narration: And once you are inside, the terminal itself starts earning.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Restaurants, shops and duty free pay the airport rent or a share of their sales. In twenty twenty-five, food and beverage brought America's airports about one point two six billion dollars, and retail and duty free almost one billion. At Los Angeles, total concessions earned about five hundred and eleven million dollars, about a quarter of its operating revenue.

Even the walls are for rent. Los Angeles earned about thirty-nine million dollars from advertising. A captive audience, waiting at the gate, with nowhere else to go. Some airports even run hotels. Across the country, airport hotels brought in about four hundred million dollars in twenty twenty-five.

And there is outside money too. Federal grants help pay for runways and terminals. The infrastructure law of twenty twenty-one set aside fourteen point five billion dollars over five years for airports, and the fifth and final installment, about two point eight nine billion dollars, has now been released. By our calculation from the FAA's grant files, federal airport grants added up to about nine billion dollars in the twenty twenty-five fiscal year.

Let me put the whole airport together. Your ticket carries a facility charge. The airlines pay rent and landing fees. Your car pays for parking, rentals or a pickup. The terminal collects from every shop and every screen. And federal grants fill in the rest. Five streams, all flowing into one public owner.

scenes.narration: So why do America's airports make money before you fly? Because an airport is not just a runway. It is a landlord, a parking operator, a shopping mall and a toll collector, all at once. And every one of those businesses gets paid long before your wheels leave the ground. So next time you land, look around. The garage, the rental counter, the coffee shop, the screens on the wall. Each one is part of how the airport pays its bills, long before anyone checks a boarding pass.
